Both sigma representations scale for every input; CASA omits the first input's SIGMA_SPECTRUM scaling, a documented correction.

An existing concatvis is the first input and is replaced atomically after the complete result is prepared. If it is also in vis, it must be the chronologically first input. Input MeasurementSets are read-only. The output records the native task and its parameters in HISTORY; it does not copy input HISTORY or a stale SORTED_TABLE cache.

Matching uses the simulation defaults, 1 Hz and 1 mas. Equivalent quantity strings or scalar quantity records are accepted. Non-default tolerances, respectname=True, timesort=True, nonempty forcesingleephemfield, and zero weight factors are refused with issue #939. The task also refuses unrepresentable scientific columns/subtables before publication. General ephemeris, reversed-channel, antenna-order conjugation, FLOAT_DATA and ancillary calibration/weather concatenation remain outside this subset.

The creation plan admits input metadata, catalogue merging, bounded batches, original uncertainty/flag columns and output writers before allocation. A failed preparation or write leaves an existing output intact.

The committed CASA fixtures exercise the public task and compare MAIN and every standard subtable, including independently changed sigma, raw row flags, pointing metadata and both input orders. They also check failed append preservation and unchanged input HISTORY. FEED row order is compared by its antenna/feed/window keys and SOURCE by source/window; longitudes modulo one turn; unspecified optional positions and empty provenance vectors as unstated metadata. A dangling CASA processor reference is corrected to -1, as described in CASA (C++) bugs.md.

The larger CASA comparisons use the unmodified m51c 12 m + 7 m pair and upstream concat tests 1 and 2. The recipe and independent comparison are in scripts/concat_parity/; the small fixture generator is task_oracle.py. The global-allocation law in creation_plan_memory.rs covers the production writer, including long pointing names and large source-model records.

On the full CASA 6.7.6-14 inputs, direct native concatenation and both CASA/native append directions preserve all 443,772 m51c rows: DATA, CORRECTED_DATA, MODEL_DATA, weights, sigma, flags, UVW and time auxiliaries agree exactly. Upstream concat tests 1 and 2 retain 95,256 and 71,442 rows; DATA and weight spectra have normalized RMS 0, with sigma differences below 1.2e-7 relative. Subtable values agree within direction/time rounding.

The final three-run serial release median for m51c was 2.14 s native and 0.142 s CASA. This is a performance limitation: the existing bounded writer rewrites all inputs, while CASA copies the first MS and appends. Improving that creation/append path remains a non-blocking performance idea.

docs.title: ALMA and ACA simulation
docs.text:
Truth class: current descriptive Last reality check: 2026-11-15 Verification: cargo test -p casa-simulation --test simalma_casa --test simalma_parameters

casars.tasks.simalma runs native ALMA/ACA observations, images each array, concatenates the interferometric data and combines them with total power. The parameter reference gives CASA's exact signature and defaults. Computation runs in Rust through the same simulator, concat, single-dish gridder, synthesis imager and image-analysis applications.

from casars.tasks import simalma

simalma(project="m51", skymodel="M51ha.fits", dryrun=False,
        antennalist=["alma.cycle6.3.cfg", "aca.cycle6.cfg"],
        totaltime="1800s", tpnant=2, tptime="7200s", pwv=0.6,
        imsize=[128, 128], mapsize="1arcmin", graphics="none")

The default dryrun=True checks the model/configurations and reports the planned exposures without publishing simulated data. overwrite=False protects an existing project. With overwrite enabled, input images, pointing files and antenna configurations inside that project are refused before the old directory can be removed.

docs.title: Observing times and total power
docs.text:
A vector totaltime supplies one exposure per configuration. A single time belongs to the highest-resolution configuration; lower-resolution 12 m configurations receive half that time, ACA 7 m twice, and an explicitly listed TP configuration four times. Array resolution strings use the same configuration resolver as simobserve. Configuration names without a cycle number work without CASA's Python-3 comparison failure.

tpnant selects the TP antenna count. Each observes for tptime; multiple antennas produce .sd.ms.Ant0, .sd.ms.Ant1, etc., with independent noise streams. pwv=0 disables thermal noise; positive values select the native ATM noise model. CASA truncates TP exposure to integer minutes; a requested TP exposure below one minute is refused instead of starting a zero-time run.

For a rectangular mosaic, TP covers one additional 12 m primary beam. For explicit pointings, it chooses the smaller of a rectangle covering all pointings plus two beams, or a two-beam patch around each pointing. Its square sampling is 0.96 * lambda / (3D). Integration is shortened when needed to visit every pointing within the requested time.

TP imaging uses the SF kernel with support 6 and nine cells per beam. Its own CASA intensity factor is gridded_major^2 / (0.96 * PB12)^2, rounded to six decimal places. This differs deliberately from simanalyze's formula. A private native concatenation feeds multiple TP antennas to the single-MS gridder, preserving weights, antenna metadata and pointings.

docs.title: Imaging and combination
docs.text:
Each configuration is imaged and analyzed with Briggs weighting. The final interferometric concatenation weights 12 m arrays by 1 and 7 m arrays by 0.34. TP is regridded onto the synthesis grid and multiplied by its primary beam before feathering; the result is divided by that beam. The project contains the array and concatenated images, differences and fidelities, TP image, .sd.image.pbscaled, .feather.image0 and .feather.image.

graphics="file", "screen" and "both" prepare complete observation, image/analysis and combination figures through the Python renderer; "none" omits them. A 12 m/7 m/two-TP-antenna run writes 14 PNGs. The final TP antenna supplies the shared TP figure names, as in CASA. Numerical products are preserved while making the summary figure. CASA's .last files are not written.

docs.title: Independent evidence
docs.text:
tools/simulation/simalma_oracle.py runs CASA 6.7.6.14 and records the compact fixture or the full upstream regression/simalma_12m_ACA_combination recipe. tools/simulation/simalma_regression.py compares every produced image and MS. The deterministic full recipe has 54 image products and five MS products; its worst image NRMS is 6.18e-6. Clean DATA is below 1e-6 NRMS.

The original noisy recipe has 52 image products and nine MS products. CASA and casa-rs use different random streams. Independent noise RMS comparisons check generation, and SIGMA is checked as MS metadata. The oracle then supplies the same native noise samples to CASA's DATA and CORRECTED_DATA for imaging. The resulting independent CASA image calculations match within 1.70e-5 NRMS. This common stochastic input is explicit; it is not a reference computed by Rust.

Other oracle controls are the already documented physical-epoch alignment, physical SF beam and full-precision fidelity floor, restored legacy Python callables, and sorted sky-model discovery. The compact project name avoids CASA's known position-angle expression bug. Exact masks and all defined pixels are checked; undefined masked non-finite samples are serialized as JSON nulls. The integrated counting law covers the whole task at two image sizes, including TP concatenation, gridding and weighted feathering.

Three serial release runs of the complete noisy upstream recipe, with no compiler running, have medians of 19.95 s native and 31.91 s CASA (1.60 times faster). This includes all observations, per-antenna TP, imaging, analysis and weighted feathering. The timing runs use each implementation's own noise stream and exclude the comparison oracle's common-noise transfer.

The graphics regression compares all 14 simalma figures and seven additional multi-array, TP, seed and feather simanalyze figures with actual CASA Matplotlib artists: image pixels, UV/ephemeris curves, labels, image/display ranges, titles, axes, pointing circles and statistical annotations. Native plot arrays share one binary payload across child tasks. Complete file/screen/both/none policies and live memory at two image sizes and spectral channel counts are tested. Plotting uses the existing native document typography.

docs.title: Native simulation imaging and analysis
docs.text:
Truth class: current descriptive Last reality check: 2026-11-15 Verification: cargo test -p casa-simulation --test simanalyze_multi_casa

casars.tasks.simanalyze composes native Rust applications to image a simulation project. It discovers the MS inputs and sky model, concatenates interferometric arrays, grids total power, initializes synthesis imaging from a supplied model, feathers, and computes the convolved sky, difference, fidelity and image statistics.

from casars.tasks import simanalyze

simanalyze(project="m51c", image=True,
           vis="$project.aca.i.ms,$project.aca.tp.sd.ms",
           modelimage="$project.sd.image", imsize=[512, 512],
           cell="0.2arcsec", analyze=True, graphics="none")

The parameter reference gives CASA's full signature and defaults. The single-array ALMA disk route is described in the tutorial evidence. Multi-array and total-power graphics use the same native plot documents as the single-array route. graphics="file", "screen", "both" and "none" select the host's output policy. TP has an analysis figure and no interferometric PSF. Feathered figures retain the original synthesis PSF and CASA's original figure-name prefix.

docs.title: Input selection and calculations
docs.text:
vis="default" discovers project MSs in sorted order and prefers their noisy counterparts. A previous <project>.concat.ms is excluded when the original arrays are present. Explicit vis accepts comma-separated paths; project-relative files take priority. $project names the project prefix, including when the native task is given an absolute project directory. Sky-model discovery prefers the first selected array's model and otherwise takes sorted candidates; skymodel selects one explicitly.

Several interferometric MSs are concatenated with CASA's (dish_diameter / first_diameter)^2 weight factors. This automatic rule requires one spectral window, a constant dish diameter within each MS, and matching constant integration times. Other combinations must be prepared explicitly. The native concat core owns its input-format limits. A repeated simulation run replaces its previous concatenation instead of appending the same observations again.

Total power uses the native single-dish application: SF support 6, nine cells per antenna primary beam, beam-area intensity scaling and cubic regridding to the requested final cell/shape. The requested cell must not exceed that SF cell. Multiple total-power MSs are refused instead of silently discarding all but CASA's last one.

modelimage initializes tclean after total-power publication, so the same invocation can create and use <project>.sd.image. A Jy/beam seed is copied privately with the Jy/pixel label that CASA's simulation wrapper supplies; its numerical seed values and the caller's original image are preserved. Other incompatible units are refused before synthesis publication.

An explicit featherimage, or the new total-power image when no seed model was supplied, is combined with the synthesis image. This follows CASA's unweighted simanalyze feather convention. Primary-beam-weighted combination belongs to simalma. Existing imager selection and gridding limits still apply; heterogeneous 12 m/7 m combination uses its mosaic response.

Numerical outputs are CASA images, with masks, WCS and beams. dryrun prepares without publishing scientific products. overwrite=False refuses existing outputs. Concat, TP and feather publications use private staging; input/output collisions are refused. logfile appends a native run report.

docs.title: Independent comparisons
docs.text:
tools/simulation/simanalyze_multi_oracle.py records CASA 6.7.6.14 products for multi-array mosaics, standalone total power, a TP seed model and feathering. The regression checks shapes, masks, coordinates, labels and defined pixels at 0.001 normalized RMS. Samples excluded by the image mask have no scientific value; their stored Fourier intermediates can differ.

The oracle restores CASA's missing legacy gentools factory and a feather callable shadowed by its simutil import. Its numerical controls are the already documented full-precision fidelity floor and the accepted SF beam correction: CASA's own C++ grdsf table is passed to CASA's beam estimator. No native output or Rust computation supplies that independent reference. --legacy-sf retains the approximate CASA beam for measuring the raw departure. On the small TP case it changes scaled intensity by about 0.11%.

tools/simulation/simanalyze_regression.py reproduces the upstream regression/sim_multi_arrays_and_TP calculation recipe from the public image/m51ha.model: 12 m, total power and 7 m observations, then two seeded simanalyze calls. It compares regenerated CASA products and records release timing. The 35 s physical epoch control at the regression's 2012 date accounts for CASA's documented TAI-labelled-as-UTC simulation bug.

The integrated counting law runs concatenation, total power, seed models and feathering at two image sizes and measures live heap against admission.

The full regenerated m51 run compares 36 native CASA images, including PSFs and residuals, with exact masks and matching coordinate references and increments. Its maximum defined- pixel NRMS is 9.18e-6; restored images and differences are below 3.5e-7, and the TP image is 1.40e-6. DATA NRMS is 8.66e-7 (12 m), 2.52e-7 (7 m) and 6.34e-8 (TP), all below the required 1e-6. The B1950 model uses its observation epoch for TP sampling and keeps its native tangent basis during synthesis imaging.

Serial release measurements of the regression's two analysis calls (three repeats, no compiler running) have medians of 6.31 s native and 12.85 s CASA, about 2.03 times faster. This measures analysis of existing MSs, including TP imaging, seed preparation, synthesis and image analysis.

docs.title: Total-power imaging with tsdimaging
docs.text:
casars.tasks.tsdimaging grids total-power spectra into a CASA image and weight image. Its 33 parameter names, order and defaults match CASA 6.7.6.14. The simulation core currently requires explicit image geometry and native spectral channels:

from casars.tasks import tsdimaging

tsdimaging(
    infiles="observation.sd.ms",
    outfile="total_power",
    imsize=[128, 128],
    cell="3arcsec",
    phasecenter="J2000 270deg -23deg",
    gridfunction="SF",
    convsupport=6,
)

The products are total_power.image and total_power.weight. Existing products require overwrite=True. The image carries its brightness unit, rest frequency, coordinates, weight-median mask and raster/kernel beam. The task returns None, as CASA does. It runs natively without a CASA installation.

Intent selection excludes flagged STATE rows. Only autocorrelations are gridded; antenna can select an antenna by ID or name, with an optional &&& suffix. Comma-separated spectral-window IDs/names select compatible windows. The task prefers corrected, then float, then observed data, with stored natural weights and the CASA two-hand combination. Four correlation products are refused. All five kernels are available: BOX, SF, GAUSS, GJINC and the telescope PB.

Default channels come from the selected intent/window. The default brightness label uses the first declared unit in corrected, float, then observed data, reading legacy UNIT before QuantumUnits. Explicit brightness labels are K or Jy/beam.

POINTING directions are converted at each integration's epoch and antenna position into the image frame. Empty POINTING falls back to FIELD; no restoring beam is invented when raster sampling is unavailable. Image and weight grids are held whole, with bounded input batches and resource admission.

Automatic geometry, multiple input sets, pointing interpolation, moving sources, spectral averaging/regridding, alternate pointing columns, clipminmax and selection forms outside this core are explicit refusals naming #938. The theoretical beam follows the previously accepted kernel corrections; CASA's model sometimes differs from the kernel its gridder uses.

CASA 6.7.6.14 comparisons cover ten small kernel cases and the named pointing boundaries. Image/weight errors are at most 3.2e-7 normalized RMS. The regenerated multi-array regression TP case agrees to 2.34e-6 (image) and 1.77e-6 (weight), with exact masks and matching WCS. The upstream native 1024-channel FLOAT_DATA test102 has identical pixels, weights and masks, with matching units and WCS. Its GBT PB beam is 718.6745 arcsec natively versus CASA's 661.8582 arcsec Airy-model estimate, the existing PB kernel-model departure. CASA reads both native products.

The public-data reproducer is tools/singledish/tsdimaging_task_parity.py --data CASATESTDATA --work WORK --native-bin TSDIMAGING --native-measures MEASURES, run under CASA's Python. Larger public datasets stay external; the small native regression tests retain their CASA-generated inputs and independent reference products.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
casa-rs supports an installer-driven suite install on macOS arm64 and Linux x86_64.

The installer published with each release:

  1. downloads the matching suite bundle
  2. installs it into a versioned suite root
  3. creates a suite-local Python environment from the bundled wheel
  4. updates the stable/rc channel links, and links the suite's task executables into ~/.local/bin

That keeps the task executables and the Python package behaving as one installed suite: the suite's Python starts the executables in its own suite's bin/.

docs.title: macOS prerequisites
docs.text:
Install the Apple command-line tools and a supported Python:

xcode-select --install
python3 --version

Release wheels are built for Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12.

docs.title: Install a stable release
docs.text:
Choose the version you want to install:

version=0.15.0
curl -fsSL "https://github.com/bglenden/casa-rs/releases/download/v${version}/install-casa-rs.sh" \
  | bash -s -- --version "$version"

That creates:

  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>
  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/stable
  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/current
  • for each task executable in the suite's bin/, such as calibrate, msexplore, imexplore, mstransform and casars-imager: ~/.local/bin/<command> and ~/.local/bin/<command>-stable

feather, immath and impv are not linked into ~/.local/bin, and there is no split command: they are CASA names that are also system commands (split is a coreutil) or generic words. Run split as mstransform split; Python starts all of them from the suite's bin/. A link in ~/.local/bin that points into the install root but no longer resolves, such as one to a command a newer suite does not have, is removed. A file of your own, or a link elsewhere, already at one of these names is left in place, and the installer says so.

docs.title: Install a release candidate side by side
docs.text:
Release candidates use the same installer, but by default they update only the rc channel links and do not take over current:

version=0.16.0-rc1
curl -fsSL "https://github.com/bglenden/casa-rs/releases/download/v${version}/install-casa-rs.sh" \
  | bash -s -- --version "$version"

That creates:

  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>
  • ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/rc
  • ~/.local/bin/<command>-rc for each command, such as ~/.local/bin/calibrate-rc

If you want the RC install to become the default suite immediately, add --activate.

docs.title: Put the suite on PATH
docs.text:
The installer links the suite's commands into ~/.local/bin. Add that directory to your shell startup file such as ~/.zshrc:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Reload the shell:

source ~/.zshrc

docs.title: Use Python from the suite
docs.text:
Activate the suite-local virtual environment:

source "$HOME/.local/opt/casa-rs/current/python/bin/activate"
python -c "import casars; print(casars.__version__)"

The suite's Python starts each task's executable from its own suite: in an install at ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>, casars.tasks.gaincal(...) runs ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>/bin/calibrate. To target a different installed suite explicitly, set:

export CASARS_SUITE_ROOT="$HOME/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>"

To run one task from another file, set its override variable, such as CASARS_CALIBRATE_BIN or CASARS_IMAGER_BIN. A wheel installed outside a suite, such as one from PyPI, needs CASARS_SUITE_ROOT (or the task's override) to run tasks; its in-process casars.tools classes need no executables.

The Python executable lookup and protocol-compatibility rules are documented in Python Compatibility.

docs.title: Stable and RC installs
docs.text:
Stable releases and release candidates can live on the same machine at the same time. The installed layout is:

~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>/
  bin/                  (every task executable of the catalog)
  python/               (the suite's virtual environment)
  wheels/
  bundle-manifest.json
~/.local/opt/casa-rs/stable -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<stable-version>
~/.local/opt/casa-rs/rc -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<rc-version>
~/.local/opt/casa-rs/current -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/<version>
~/.local/bin/
  calibrate -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/current/bin/calibrate
  calibrate-stable -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/stable/bin/calibrate
  calibrate-rc -> ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/rc/bin/calibrate
  ...                   (the same links for each executable in bin/,
                         except feather, immath and impv)

Switch the default suite by repointing ~/.local/opt/casa-rs/current, re-running the installer with --activate, or keep multiple installs in place and choose one explicitly with CASARS_SUITE_ROOT or that suite's Python virtual environment.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
If you are working from a checkout instead of a published release asset, install Rust and build locally:

curl https://sh.rustup.rs -sSf | sh
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"
cargo build --release --workspace --bins

A Python package installed from the checkout (pip install -e crates/casars-python) runs the newest debug or release build of each task executable in that checkout's target/ (or $CARGO_TARGET_DIR), unless CASARS_SUITE_ROOT or the task's override is set. A task whose executable is not built names the cargo build -p <package> --bin <executable> that builds it.

To package a local release-style bundle, run:

scripts/build-python-dist.sh dist/python
scripts/package-suite-bundle.sh \
  --version "$(sed -n 's/^version = \"\\(.*\\)\"/\\1/p' Cargo.toml | head -n 1)" \
  --platform "$(scripts/install-suite.sh --print-platform)" \
  --bin-dir target/release \
  --wheel-dir dist/python \
  --out-dir dist/python

To build, bundle, and install the current checkout in one step, run:

just install-local

just install-local runs just install-local-suite. Use --force for an ad-hoc reinstall of the same checkout version:

just install-local -- --force

To install a published release suite without rebuilding the checkout or rerunning release verification gates, run:

just install-release 0.17.0

docs.title: Provider Contracts and Schema Bundles
docs.text:
This document defines the contract model between functionality providers and their consumers:

  • the Python package casars
  • the task executables of the application catalog, run directly from the command line

ADR-0017 makes these the product surfaces; casa-rs has no separate launcher, terminal UI, native GUI, or interactive browser sessions.

The goal is to keep one source of truth for each provider surface while still allowing different transports.

docs.title: Core Rule
docs.text:
The canonical boundary contract is a versioned, typed provider bundle.

  • Providers own request/result, object, and private adapter semantics. The shared catalog owns reusable public parameter concepts.
  • Rust types implement that contract inside the provider.
  • Generated machine artifacts publish that contract to the CLI, Python parity checks, and test fixtures.
  • Presentation hints belong in the same schema bundle as annotations. They do not replace the semantic contract.

JSON and JSON Schema remain valid machine transports and projections. They are not the semantic model itself, and the user-editable parameter profile format is sparse TOML.

The source of truth is therefore not:

  • raw CLI flags
  • hand-maintained Python wrappers
  • an app-local default or alias table

It is the checked catalog plus the self-contained provider schema bundle that embeds the concepts referenced by its surface definition.

docs.title: Surface Kinds
docs.text: A provider bundle advertises one of two surface kinds (ProviderSurfaceKind). Every parameter surface is a task; the profile SurfaceKind has the single variant task.

docs.title: Task Surfaces
docs.text:
Task surfaces are one-shot operations with a request and a result.

Examples:

  • calibrate
  • casars-imager

Machine-facing shape:

  • --protocol-info
  • --json-schema
  • --json-run <SOURCE>

The protocol is request/result oriented. CLI flags and Python wrappers are projections of the same task contract.

A task SurfaceDefinition also binds its public parameter names to the shared ParameterCatalog and adapts the resolved set into the provider's private, idiomatic Rust request.

docs.title: Object Surfaces
docs.text:
Object surfaces expose stateful handles with constructors, properties, methods, and lifecycle operations.

The object surfaces are the CASA tool classes of casars.tools (ADR-0017). They include simulator (CASA's sm), measures (me), quanta (qa), componentlist (cl), image (ia), coordsys (cs), table (tb), msmetadata (msmd) and ms. The classes use CASA's method names, parameter order and effective defaults. Python uses them in process through the native extension. One bundle, casars_data_objects (casars.data.schema_bundle(), protocol version 1), describes them all; its tool entries all come from one list of the casars.tools classes, and each names its own module in its projection entry (Compatibility). casars.simutil, a port of CASA's simutil helper class rather than a CASA tool, is not an object surface and is not in the bundle.

A CASA tool's entry carries:

  • each method's parameters as a JSON Schema object whose properties give the value kind and the installed CASA binding's default (a parameter without a default is required); CASA's any parameters refer to the shared CasaQuantityArgument and CasaMeasureArgument components, and its record parameters are JSON objects;
  • each method's result kind (a boolean, string, record, list of strings or array of numbers);
  • in projections.python, the tool's module and class and the parameter order of its constructor (keyword-only casa-rs controls) and of each method, which JSON Schema's properties do not keep;
  • in annotations.python, whether casa-rs implements each method.

The Python tests compare each tool's entry with inspect.signature of the class and with the installed CASA binding.

Machine-facing shape:

  • a versioned schema bundle describing constructors, properties, methods, and common value types
  • no standalone executable required

docs.title: Bundle Shape
docs.text:
Each provider surface exposes one canonical schema bundle. The bundle contains at least:

  1. protocol
  2. protocol name
  3. protocol version
  4. surface kind: task or object
  5. semantic contract
  6. tasks: operations with request/result schemas
  7. objects: constructors, properties, methods, lifecycle operations
  8. parameter contract where the surface is parameterized
  9. shared ParameterCatalog concepts
  10. the task SurfaceDefinition
  11. parameter bindings, defaults, roles and validation
  12. shared component schemas
  13. reusable logical value definitions referenced across operations
  14. annotations
  15. labels, descriptions, ordering, groupings, examples, advanced/basic and hidden flags, units, and other presentation metadata
  16. projection metadata where needed
  17. CLI flag names and positional rules
  18. Python parameter names

The semantic layer is authoritative. Annotations and projections may add presentation or mapping metadata, but they must not change semantic meaning.

Task providers use the shared ProviderContractEnvelope<Semantic, Schemas> implementation in casa-provider-contracts. The envelope owns protocol identity, semantic operations, reusable components, annotations, projections, and embedded parameter surfaces. Provider crates supply only their typed domain schemas and operations. The common validator rejects wrong surface kinds, missing parameter surfaces, noncanonical actions, duplicate operations, protocol metadata errors, and semantic/flattened schema drift.

docs.title: Application Catalog and Launching
docs.text:
casa-provider-contracts also owns the single ApplicationCatalog. Every parameter surface has exactly one task-application entry that references the surface by stable ID, and every application is a task: each catalog entry is one task surface. Display name, category, and protocol family are projected from the referenced surface rather than copied into another inventory. Each application adds only executable/package identity (launch), its explicit override variable, the kinds of dataset it reads, and packaging visibility (include_in_suite); an entry carrying any other field is refused. Several surfaces may share one executable, a family whose first word names the surface: imhead and imstat run imexplore; plotms runs msexplore; split runs mstransform; and gaincal, bandpass, applycal, fluxscale, and gencal run calibrate, whose own calibrate surface is its default.

casa_provider_contracts::resolve_task_executable is the one search for the file a task runs; Python reaches it through casars._core. The first step that applies decides:

  1. the task's override variable (override_env, CASARS_<APP>_BIN, such as CASARS_IMAGER_BIN or CASARS_CALIBRATE_BIN);
  2. a suite root, CASARS_SUITE_ROOT or else the installed suite the Python package belongs to (the installer's environment is <suite>/python, beside <suite>/bin and bundle-manifest.json), whose bin/ holds the executable;
  3. a development checkout: the newest debug or release build of the executable under the workspace the package was built from, in $CARGO_TARGET_DIR or target/.

A step that applies but lacks the file is an error naming what it lacked, and never falls through to a later step, so an installed suite never runs a checkout's build. A missing development build is reported with the cargo build -p <package> --bin <executable> that makes it. Nothing is run through cargo, PATH is not searched, and the caller's own path (current_exe) is not consulted. Python, packaging scripts, and the suite inventory all project from this catalog.

docs.title: Parameter Catalog and Surface Definitions
docs.text:
ADR-0006 defines the common parameter model and current-only profiles.

ParameterCatalog entries describe reusable concepts:

  • stable semantic ID and canonical CASA-facing name
  • value type, normalization, base constraints, semantic equality, and, where applicable, unit dimension
  • semantic role and persistence class
  • meaning and public documentation

A canonical name has one meaning across surfaces. Reuse is by semantic concept, not by matching strings. Two parameters with different meanings must not share a catalog concept even when a legacy CLI happens to spell them alike.

ParameterBinding describes one concept's use on one surface:

  • absent, literal, or pure conditional default
  • required and activation predicates
  • provably narrowing refinements and projection metadata
  • an optional context role consistent with the concept's semantic role

Concept roles are part of the contract. A path that is safe as an input does not become an output merely because both serialize as strings. Runtime-only controls such as executable overrides, progress paths, telemetry, and Last controls are explicitly non-persistable. There are no run-time confirmations: CASA's own parameters, such as overwrite, are the consent to replace or change data.

A task SurfaceDefinition maps the resolved CASA-named parameter set into a one-shot provider invocation.

Every optional parameter has an explicit default. Conditional defaults depend only on other parameters and form an acyclic graph. Dataset-derived context is an explicit suggestion or override, never an undeclared default.

docs.title: Sparse Parameter Documents
docs.text:
The human interchange format is versioned sparse TOML. The [casars] table identifies format version, surface ID, surface kind (always task), and contract version. The [parameters] table contains required values and normalized semantic differences from current defaults. Values containing non-finite floats, complex or NumPy scalars, explicitly typed empty arrays, or zero-dimensional arrays are instead stored in an optional [typed_parameters] table, as JSON strings containing recursively tagged parameter values. This keeps complex values distinct from ordinary records and allows profiles to round-trip them without reserving any record key.

A saved profile must match the current task, format, and profile version. Recreate stale profiles using the current parameters. Adding an optional parameter can leave the version alone: a saved file uses its current default. Change the marker when a file can no longer be read with its intended meaning.

Parameter documents do not support includes, environment or shell expansion, remote URLs, or executable expressions. Relative task paths resolve against the selected workspace or process current directory, not the profile file's parent. See Task Parameter Profiles for the user contract and managed-state lifecycle.

docs.title: Canonical schema discovery
docs.text:
--json-schema emits a machine representation of the canonical provider bundle, including the parameter catalog and applicable surface definition.

Consumers project from the embedded canonical surface in-process. Providers expose no second schema-discovery action or cached presentation payload.

Every one-shot task binary answers --json-schema, --protocol-info and --json-run <SOURCE> through the shared task front end below, which owns stdin and file ingestion, JSON decoding and encoding, and the typed reply. A binary keeps only its typed execution callback.

docs.title: The shared task front end and typed replies
docs.text:
casa-task-runtime::TaskFrontEnd is the one entry every task binary's main calls, including the family binaries that host several surfaces. A surface's choices take their canonical names (--preset amplitude_vs_time), and every flag it declares, short ones such as msexplore's -o included, reaches its parameter. The front end is generic over the binary's execution callback and owns the surface's declared flags, the base sources, --workspace, --unset, --save-params, --no-save-last, the non-executing --show, --template (also --profile-template), --describe and --validate, and the machine actions. A spelling the surface declares is always its parameter, so imregrid's --template names its template image and --profile-template gives its profile. A family binary's first word names the surface it runs, such as imexplore imstat, mstransform split or calibrate gaincal; the first hosted surface runs otherwise. A --json-run request names its surface itself; the fixed_args that imhead, imstat and the calibration surfaces carry repeat it as the first word, while split and plotms carry none. The callback reads the resolved values into the binary's typed request through TaskInvocation's typed reads, and TaskInvocation::is_set tells a value the run sets from a default. What a command line prints is the callback's text (msexplore's summary in the user's format), with notes such as msexplore's flag-edit line on stderr; --json-run carries the value and result instead.

The binary's main owns the process. It reads the logging configuration from the environment (CasaLoggingConfig::from_env) and passes it, with its arguments, how the process enters a directory (std::env::set_current_dir) and its standard output and error, to TaskFrontEnd::main. The front end reads no environment variable and changes no process state itself (ADR-0016): it applies the logging flags, and for a run installs logging that writes to the stderr it was handed and to a log table only when one is named. An action that runs nothing installs no logging, so a bad CASA_RS_LOG_* setting refuses only a run.

A command-line run enters its workspace (--workspace, the current directory otherwise) before the task starts, as a Python task call starts the executable in its workspace. Every relative path the run names then resolves in the workspace: inputs, products, and paths inside a parameter's text, such as imstat's region file or the image in immoments' mask expression. The files the controls name (--params, --save-params, a log table) are read and written from where the command was run, before it enters. A --json-run runs where its caller started it.

--json-run SOURCE takes a TaskRunRequest, {"surface": ..., "values": {...}} with the CASA-named values the caller set, and resolves it against the surface's contract inside the binary. For values JSON cannot express directly, the request may also contain a typed_values map of recursively tagged parameter values. A parameter may occur in only one of values and typed_values; typed inputs are accepted only for variant parameters and pass the same validation as plain inputs. The binary writes one TaskReply to stdout:

  • {"status": "succeeded", "surface", "value", "result"}, where value is what CASA's task returns (null for None), kept ahead of the provider's full result, from which products are projected;
  • {"status": "failed", "surface", "kind", "message", "parameter"?}, where kind is validation (refused before anything changed), execution, or interrupted: the task caught an interrupt, stopped at its next safe point and published nothing, as casars-imager does on SIGINT.

The exit status agrees with the reply: 0 for success, 2 for a validation failure, 1 for an execution failure and 130 for an interrupted run. classify_task_exit reads a finished process from its exit status and stdout alone, never stderr, and keeps a launch failure, a signal and a malformed reply distinct from the task's own failures. A provider contract carries both schemas under semantic.front_end.

A surface with a managed_output contract names the decoder that reads its provider result (calibration-report-v1, imager-run-v1, simobserve-run-v1): the reply's result is that result, from which the completion decoder projects products and the summary. Nothing is injected into the binary's arguments to ask for it.

Last has one owner on each path: a command line run of a binary records Last before the callback and Last Successful only after success, unless --no-save-last; --json-run reads and writes neither, so Python task calls save none. Every Python task call is one invocation shape: the executable the resolver names, the surface's fixed_args, then --json-run - with the values the call set on stdin. Python passes the task's log lines to sys.stderr as they arrive and classifies the reply through casars._core. A success returns a TaskCompletion carrying the reply's value and the products the decoder projects. A validation reply raises TaskParameterError, a ValueError whose completion's status is refused; anything else raises TaskExecutionError, whose completion's status is failed, interrupted, signalled or malformed_reply. A value the contract refuses when Python resolves the call raises ValueError before anything starts, or TypeError for a value of the wrong type.

A succeeded reply's value is CASA's return value as a tagged CasaValue (casa-provider-contracts): none, bool, int, float (non-finite values as "nan", "-nan", "inf" and "-inf"), complex (with real and imaginary components in the same float representation), string, list, an ordered dict whose keys are strings or integers, and typed arrays (bool_array, int_array with dtype int32 or int64, uint64_array, float_array with float32 or float64, complex_array, str_array) that carry their shape and their data in column-major (Fortran) order. casars._core rebuilds Python's types and NumPy arrays from it, so a CASA-signature wrapper returns what CASA returns. tools/casa-compat/record_casa_returns.py records the structure of CASA's own return values (resources/casa-compat/casa-6.7.6.14/returns.json), which the image, MeasurementSet and calibration task tests compare against.

docs.title: Shared Versioned Component Schemas
docs.text:
Protocol-independent basic types have versioned shared schemas, reused across task and object surfaces rather than redefined per provider. Component families include:

  • scalar values
  • bool
  • integer and floating-point values
  • complex values
  • strings
  • array values
  • dtype / primitive type
  • shape
  • axis-order semantics
  • fixed-shape and variable-shape array forms
  • record values
  • named fields with nested values
  • keyword maps
  • table keywords
  • column keywords
  • image misc/info-like nested metadata maps
  • error envelopes
  • stable error code
  • message
  • optional structured details
  • file/path references
  • file path
  • directory path
  • path role hints for validation

These shared schemas are versioned explicitly:

  • a versioned family name for the logical type set
  • stable $defs / component identifiers within that family
  • additive extension within a compatible protocol version
  • explicit protocol-version bumps for breaking shape changes

The logical schema describes semantics, not one transport encoding. For example, Python maps image planes directly to NumPy arrays in-process.

docs.title: Projection Rules
docs.text: All consumers project from the same canonical schema bundle.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
CLI parsing is a projection from the semantic contract plus CLI annotation metadata such as flag names and positional rules.

CLI flags are not the source of truth.

Each task executable's command line, through the shared task front end, also projects the common Defaults, Last, Last Successful, explicit profile, reset (--unset), save (--save-params), and no-save (--no-save-last) source operations, and the non-executing --show, --template, --describe and --validate. Invocation starts from Defaults unless a source is explicit.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Python stays ergonomic and typed, but its wrappers and docs are checked against the canonical schema bundle so signatures and enums cannot drift.

For task surfaces, generated Python callables start the task's executable with the canonical --json-run - transport; Python does not host a second provider protocol engine. For object surfaces, Python binds directly in-process.

casars.parameters exposes the common typed task profile, while generated task-specific wrappers delegate through the same runtime. Python must not keep a second implementation of defaults.

docs.title: Surface inventory
docs.text: Every catalog surface is a task surface; the generated parameter reference lists them. The object surfaces above are not parameter-profile surfaces.

docs.title: Implementation Guidance
docs.text:
• Define typed Rust structs and enums that serialize exactly to the canonical schema bundle shapes.
  • Define reusable catalog concepts once and bind them explicitly on every parameterized task surface.
  • Generate schema output from those types rather than hand-maintaining schema JSON.
  • Keep presentation hints in the schema bundle as annotations.
  • Keep protocol names and protocol versions explicit and machine-checkable.
  • Add CI parity tests so catalog coverage, wrappers, docs, sparse profiles, and projections cannot drift from the canonical schema bundle.

This preserves one source of truth while supporting direct Rust APIs, the Python package, and the task executables.

docs.title: Rust API
docs.text:
The generated Rust API documentation is published alongside this site at:

  • Rust API reference

The rustdoc tree is generated from source documentation comments with cargo doc --workspace --no-deps.

docs.title: Task Parameter Profiles
docs.text:
Truth class: normative user contract Status: implemented Verification: just docs-check; <executable> --help (for example imexplore --help)

casa-rs uses one parameter model for its one-shot tasks. A profile can be loaded by a task executable's command line or manipulated from Python without changing the parameter names or their meaning. Every parameter surface is a task (ADR-0017).

This guide describes the implemented interface from ADR-0006, including current-only surface evolution. Provider JSON requests, results, and progress remain machine transports; TOML is the sole human-authored parameter-profile format.

The generated parameter reference lists every cataloged task surface, its parameters, and their canonical concept revisions, types, units, defaults, groups, and summaries.

docs.title: Sparse TOML format
docs.text:
Parameter profiles are UTF-8 TOML with an ASCII-oriented syntax. They are designed to paste cleanly into Markdown:

[casars]
format = 1
surface = "tclean"
kind = "task"
contract = 42

[parameters]
vis = "data/target.ms"
imagename = "products/target"
imsize = 1024
cell = "0.2arcsec"
field = "target"
spw = "0:32~255"
specmode = "cube"
weighting = "briggs"
niter = 10000
threshold = "2mJy"

Only required values and values that differ semantically from current defaults are written. Resetting a field removes its override and reveals the current default. Quantities are compared by value and dimension, so equivalent values such as "0.001Jy" and "1mJy" do not create a false override.

Files do not execute code. Includes, URL loading, environment expansion, shell expressions, and executable selection are not part of the format. Unknown, duplicate, inactive, or wrong-surface parameters are errors with source locations where possible. A compound value is replaced as one value; profiles are not recursive merge patches.

Use the version emitted by the current executable's profile template. Older and newer profile versions are rejected with an error. To use an old file, start from the current template and copy the values you still need, using current parameter names. An omitted optional value uses the current default.

Relative dataset and product paths resolve against the explicit workspace or the process current directory. They do not resolve relative to the profile file merely because the file lives elsewhere.

docs.title: Native EVLA AW convolution functions
docs.text:
With gridder = "awproject", aw_cf_source = "casa-import" is the default and requires an explicit cfcache input directory. CASA CFS_/WTCFS_ cells are imported read-only; auto does not select or create a cache.

Select aw_cf_source = "native-evla" to use the frozen homogeneous 25 m EVLA dish model without CASA at runtime. Supply evla_surface (the explicit dish surface input file), native_cf_cache (a separate private cache directory), native_cf_working_size, native_cf_oversampling, native_cf_cache_bytes, and native_cf_maximum_cells. Sampling and resource bounds are explicit request parameters, not inferred from a cache's contents. The native cache is not CASA-readable and cannot also be supplied as cfcache.

native_cf_policy defaults to "reuse-only": an incomplete or invalid cache fails without generation. "generate-missing" creates absent cells and retains valid completed cells; corruption remains an error. "regenerate" explicitly replaces all requested cells. Neither source falls back to the other. These parameters are available through the same CLI flags, task JSON, sparse profiles, and generated Python wrapper. Profiles store the requested paths/action/bounds, not compiled plans, generated cells, cache inventory, or publication state. This exposes the frozen EVLA case, not general telescope support.

The native cells follow tclean's terms as CASA's AWProjectFT reads them: aterm, psterm, wbawp (cells at each window's frequency, or at the image reference frequency alone; without the aperture CASA drops it), conjbeams (the weight cell's conjugate beam) and wprojplanes (one plane is co-planar). An imported CASA cache already holds the cells its run made; with it only conjbeams changes the run, choosing the cell each sample grids with.

docs.title: Sources and precedence
docs.text:
Every task run resolves its parameters from exactly one base source:

  • Defaults
  • Last attempted
  • Last successful
  • an explicit profile file

Resolution order is:

current defaults
  -> one base source
  -> explicit CLI or Python overrides

Dataset-derived suggestions are explicit values, not hidden defaults. Choosing another base source replaces the base rather than merging into it.

Command-line and Python calls start from Defaults unless a source is specified. A missing managed profile is distinct from an unreadable or invalid one: asking for Last when no Last file exists is reported as missing, and a present corrupt Last file is reported as an error and is never silently replaced by Defaults.

docs.title: Managed Last files
docs.text:
By default, managed state lives under the workspace:

<workspace>/.casa-rs/parameters/<surface-id>/last.toml
<workspace>/.casa-rs/parameters/<surface-id>/last-successful.toml

Last records command-line runs. Last attempted is saved after resolution and validation, immediately before execution. Last successful changes only after a successful result. Cancellation or failure leaves Last successful unchanged. --no-save-last skips both writes for one run.

A Python task call saves neither file; reading an existing Last (parameters.last(...)) and writing one explicitly (TaskParameters.write_last()) remain available. A task executable's --json-run, the path Python's calls take, reads and writes no Last either. Last therefore has one owner: the task front end, for a command-line run of a task executable.

casa-task-runtime::ParameterRuntime owns source resolution and managed Last persistence; the CLI and Python projections call that boundary rather than keeping their own Last-state logic.

Set CASA_RS_STATE_DIR to redirect managed state in automation. This changes the state location, not the workspace used for relative task paths.

Automatic Last updates never overwrite an explicit profile file.

docs.title: CLI contract
docs.text:
Each task runs from its own executable, which the application catalog names (calibrate, imexplore, casars-imager, simobserve, ...). Every task executable runs on the shared task front end in casa-task-runtime, so all take the same command line; --help prints it with the surface's parameters.

<executable> [SURFACE] [SOURCE] [OVERRIDES] [CONTROLS]
<executable> [SURFACE] --show [SOURCE] [OVERRIDES] [--save-params FILE]
<executable> [SURFACE] --template | --profile-template | --describe [NAME] | --validate FILE
<executable> --json-run <SOURCE> | --json-schema | --protocol-info
  • SURFACE is the first word of a family executable, which hosts several surfaces: calibrate (calibrate, applycal, gaincal, bandpass, fluxscale, gencal), imexplore (imhead, imstat), msexplore (msexplore, plotms) and mstransform (mstransform, split). Without it the first hosted surface runs. Other executables host one surface.
  • SOURCE is exactly one of --defaults (the default), --last, --last-successful or --params FILE.
  • OVERRIDES are the flags the surface declares, or --unset NAME, which removes an override.
  • CONTROLS are --workspace DIR (where relative paths resolve and Last and Last Successful live), --save-params FILE (also write the run's resolved sparse profile) and --no-save-last.

For example:

calibrate gaincal --ms ngc5921.ms --out ngc5921.G0 --refant VA15 --solint inf
imexplore imstat --last --show --save-params imstat.toml

The non-executing actions resolve the same sources and overrides and run nothing: --show prints the resolved parameters, and with --save-params FILE saves them as a sparse profile; --template writes a documented example with defaults and units in comments, whose commented defaults are not active overrides; --describe [NAME] describes the surface or one parameter; --validate FILE checks a profile against the surface. Overrides use the generated CLI flag spellings listed in the generated parameter reference, or the parameter's own name, such as --vis or --threshold; some surfaces declare their own spellings, such as calibrate's --ms and --out.

A list's command-line form is comma-separated (--archivefiles a.exp,b.exp). A flag repeated for a list without a fixed size adds to it, so --archivefile a.exp --archivefile b.exp names both archives; any other repeated flag takes its last value. A path list given as one string, on the command line, in a profile or in a --json-run request, is split at its commas before each path is normalized, so every route names the same paths. A refused value names its parameter, on the command line as in a reply's parameter.

There are no run-time confirmations. CASA's own parameters are the consent: overwrite=true replaces a product, and a task that changes data in place does so, as in CASA. Where CASA guards a change, casa-rs does too, for example applycal and flagdata saving the flags to a new flag version first (flagbackup, default on). No task takes a confirmation flag.

The machine actions (--protocol-info, --json-schema, --json-run) are the same on every task executable; --json-run gives a typed reply (provider contracts). A spelling the surface declares is always its parameter: imregrid's --template is its template image, so there --profile-template writes the profile. A run started from a task's command line enters its --workspace first, so its relative paths resolve there, as they do for a Python call in its workspace.

docs.title: Python contract
docs.text:
The Python API exposes the same profile model:

from casars import parameters, tasks

p = parameters.defaults("tclean", workspace="project")
p.update(
    vis="data/target.ms",
    imagename="products/target",
    imsize=1024,
    cell="0.2arcsec",
)
p.save("profiles/target-imaging.toml")

result = p.run()                          # in the draft's workspace
result = tasks.run("tclean", p, niter=0)  # the draft, with one more value

Companion constructors are parameters.last(...), parameters.last_successful(...), and parameters.load(path, ...). TaskParameters supports mapping-style updates, reset(name), reload(), save(path), provider_invocation(), and run(**values). As a mapping, a draft holds the parameters that have a value, so a loaded profile runs through a CASA-named wrapper, in the current directory, as tasks.gaincal(**parameters.load(path)). The invocation exposes the provider protocol name/version, the arguments (the surface's fixed arguments, then --json-run -), and the exact canonical request stdin.

tasks.run(task, parameters=None, /, *, workspace=None, **values) accepts every catalog task. It starts from the draft, or Defaults, sets values, and runs in workspace: the draft's, or the current directory. The CASA-named wrappers take the surface's parameters and run in the current directory. Each call starts the task's own executable, found by the resolver (Install), with --json-run -, and passes its log lines to sys.stderr as they arrive. The log reaches stderr at the logging configuration's threshold, WARN by default; CASA_RS_LOG_STDERR_PRIORITY=INFO also shows a task's INFO lines, such as its start and completion. Ctrl-C (KeyboardInterrupt) is passed to the task as SIGINT; the task has ten seconds to stop before it is killed, and the KeyboardInterrupt is then raised again.

A value the contract refuses, such as a parameter its gridder does not read, raises ValueError before anything starts, or TypeError when the value has the wrong type. A task that refuses its parameters itself, such as an input that does not exist, raises casars.tasks.TaskParameterError, a ValueError; one that starts and does not succeed raises casars.tasks.TaskExecutionError, a RuntimeError. Both carry the .completion, whose status is refused, failed, interrupted, signalled or malformed_reply, with its message and the parameter it names. TaskBinaryNotFoundError, a FileNotFoundError, says what the resolver lacked; TaskInvocationError means the executable could not be started, and TaskResultError that a success's result was malformed. tasks.run returns a TaskCompletion with the command run, its workspace, returncode, stdout (the reply), stderr (the log), the provider_invocation, CASA's return value from the reply, and the declared products (result, products); result projection remains Rust-owned.

The CASA-named wrappers and their type stubs are generated from the catalog, under casars.tasks; there is no second provider-specific task API. A surface that names its CASA task (casa_task; every surface but the casa-rs tasks calibrate, msexplore and msconvert, and plotms) has CASA's exact signature: CASA's parameters in CASA's order, positional or by keyword, with CASA's defaults, then casa-rs's own controls, keyword-only. Its wrapper returns CASA's value: imstat's statistics dictionary with NumPy arrays, immath's True, flagdata's summary dictionary in summary mode and {} in its other modes, flagmanager's version list in list mode, gaincal's and bandpass's tables and selected data, fluxscale's flux densities, None for most tasks. A parameter casa-rs does not implement yet is taken only at CASA's default and refused at any other value, naming its issue; the wrapper's docstring lists them. The other wrappers take keyword arguments and return the TaskCompletion. CASA compatibility compares each surface with its CASA task.

docs.title: What profiles intentionally exclude
docs.text:
• casars.tools.image and casars.tools.table object-handle lifecycle
  • progress files, executable overrides, Last controls, and telemetry
  • saved region and mask mutations, which are dataset artifacts
  • an exact resolved historical replay record

If exact run replay is needed, record a separate run manifest containing the fully resolved invocation and versions. A sparse profile records user intent under the current contract and defaults.

docs.title: ADR-0006: One parameter model and current sparse profiles
docs.text:
Status: accepted Date: 2026-11-12 Truth class: normative

The CLI, Python, and task providers share Rust definitions for parameter names, types, defaults, normalization, and validation. Share concepts by meaning; each task supplies its own bindings and defaults. Runtime controls such as executable selection and telemetry stay out of saved parameters.

Profiles are sparse TOML. They store required values and explicit differences from defaults. Provider JSON is a machine transport. The common task runtime owns resolution and any managed Last state; ordinary Python task calls leave Last alone.

A profile must name the current task and use the current file format and task profile version. Refuse stale files and tell the user to recreate them. Bump the marker only when an existing profile can no longer be interpreted as intended. An added optional parameter can use its default. The former migration and history policy is superseded by ADR-0020.

See Task Parameter Profiles for the format and Provider Contracts for the current implementation.

docs.title: ADR-0008: Casacore storage and bounded MeasurementSet writes
docs.text:
Status: accepted

Date: 2026-07-18

Reaffirmed: 2026-08-26

Amended: 2026-10-09, on owner direction: casa-rs writes nothing into a MeasurementSet that CASA does not write.

Amended: 2026-10-10, on owner direction: in-place mutation waits for a table lock another process holds, as casacore does, instead of being refused at once.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
CASA interoperability depends on the casacore table data model and persisted data-manager metadata, not on a casa-rs-specific row layout. MeasurementSets may be created by CASA with different valid storage-manager bindings, tile shapes, hypercube layouts, and variable array shapes. At the same time, production writers must not materialize a large MAIN table or retain payloads proportional to its row count.

Earlier design discussion considered rollback or snapshot machinery for large writes. No product requirement currently calls for transactional rollback, historical generations, or user-visible snapshots, and those mechanisms would add persistent state and recovery complexity to the interoperability boundary.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Table row, column, and cell accessors remain the primary public table-data interface. A column's storage manager is a strategic creation-time choice. Opening an existing table reads its persisted data-manager sequence, type, columns, properties, and tile or hypercube metadata; mutation preserves those bindings rather than replacing them with casa-rs conventions.

casa-tables natively reads the supported standard casacore managers and writes their canonical formats. A manager implemented only by an external casacore plugin may be reported as unsupported. TiledShapeStMan uses one hypercube for each distinct cell shape, and rows with the same shape reuse that hypercube. Unused planned shapes do not create payload files or row maps.

MAIN-table producers use one MeasurementSetWritePlan and one MeasurementSetWriteSession. The immutable plan names every owned scalar and array column, derives tile geometry from the existing storage planner, fixes batch and queue sizes, reserves every scalar and array writer buffer, and reports the maximum modeled writer-owned resident bytes. The session streams typed cells, installs the planned columns, and reports rows, bytes, producer time, bounded-queue wait, assembly, physical-write, and finalization time.

Creation uses a sibling staging directory and publishes it only after a complete interoperable table has been written. In-place mutation holds casacore's table write lock from its first change until it completes or is abandoned, as CASA does. When another process holds a lock on the table, in-place mutation waits for it, as casacore does by default: the waiter adds its process id to the request list in table.lock, so that a holder using casacore's AutoLocking releases its lock at its next inspection, and the wait is logged when it starts, periodically while it lasts, and when it ends. casacore throttles those inspections, so a holder that uses the table only lightly may keep its lock until it closes the table. The wait blocks in the kernel, as casacore's does, so the kernel refuses a wait that would deadlock, such as the second of two processes upgrading their read locks, and that writer fails. A writer whose table was opened without locking and that finds another process wrote the table while it waited is refused, because what it read beforehand is stale. A save that locks several tables of a MeasurementSet never waits while it holds another table's lock, and is refused before writing when another process wrote a table it released to wait. A released write lock publishes the table as persisted (rows, columns and one change counter per data manager, read from table.dat). An in-place writer publishes every table it started to write, so a write interrupted part way is announced; a locked table handle publishes when it wrote the table under its write lock, even if it reloaded the table afterwards, and publishes nothing when nothing reached the disk, as casacore's PlainTable::putFile announces each write it makes. A conflicting handle in the same process is refused at once, because it may belong to the waiting thread. casa-rs does not yet release a lock it holds when another process requests it (#694); a waiter, CASA's or casa-rs's, waits until a casa-rs holder, such as an imaging run with its retained read locks, finishes. On a file system without lock support (fcntl refused with ENOLCK, or ENOTSUP as on macOS SMB mounts) the table is used unlocked, with a warning, as casacore does for ENOLCK; there is then no cross-process exclusion. casa-rs adds nothing of its own to a MeasurementSet: no table keywords, marker files, generations or identities. An interrupted in-place write may leave cells partly written, as an interrupted CASA write does; rerunning the producing task recomputes them.

The persistence layer does not provide rollback, snapshot generations, journaling, or copy-on-write recovery. Such a feature requires a new concrete product requirement and a separate architecture decision.

This applies explicitly to imaging MODEL_DATA and CORRECTED_DATA. Prediction writes selected cells in place under the exact source-scoped table lock. The writer retains at most one array cell, persists that cell through the selected-row/selected-column table seam, and discards its cache entry before accepting another row; it does not materialize MAIN rows or the full column. Unrelated MeasurementSets may therefore progress concurrently while two live writers for the same source remain mutually exclusive. Successful completion flushes the column and releases the lock. An interrupted write may leave partial derived values, which the next run recomputes. Full-column staging copies, backup columns, content digests, and rollback are prohibited unless a later concrete requirement demonstrates that CASA-compatible in-place behavior is inadequate and separately accounts for the I/O and storage cost.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• CASA-generated MeasurementSets need not follow casa-rs creation conventions to be readable or safely mutated.
  • Memory use is planned from the real column shapes and writer buffers rather than a fixed row-count heuristic.
  • New-output failure is isolated before publication. In-place failure may have written some cells, as in CASA; rerunning the task recomputes them.
  • A MeasurementSet written by casa-rs carries only what CASA would write, so CASA and casa-rs can each open the other's output without preparation.
  • Flag-version tables remain an explicit domain feature of flagmanager; they are not a transaction or rollback mechanism for general table writes.
  • Storage changes require Rust-read/Rust-write and C++-read/C++-write interoperability evidence, including heterogeneous TiledShapeStMan data when that path changes.

docs.title: ADR-0009: Mathematical imaging architecture
docs.text: Status: accepted Date: 2026-08-18 Truth class: normative Supersedes: Superseded by: ADR-0016, in part (the migration rules and the attestation and identity wording, since removed from this record)

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Imaging behavior was distributed across application dispatch, mode-specific preparation, imaging modules, solver controllers, and product writers. Continuum, spectral-line, mosaic, W/AW-projection, MT-MFS, CPU, and Metal paths repeated or reinterpreted scientific choices. Geometry, measurement-equation terms, weighting, normalization and products had no enforceable dependency boundaries. A new vocabulary alone would permit the same architecture to reappear behind new names.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: CASA-RS imaging follows one normative mathematical and ownership architecture.

docs.title: Ownership and dependency direction
docs.text:
Application and frontend layers may version-migrate and validate request syntax, select a Resource Policy, invoke compile and run, and present results. They do not query devices, evaluate scientific capability/backend eligibility, select gridders or solvers, construct science caches, allocate imaging work buffers, or define or write scientific products.

Scientific definitions depend on no frontend, execution backend, or device API. Observation and MeasurementSet interoperability are isolated behind observation interfaces. Reconstruction depends on Measurement Operator and Normal State contracts rather than casacore or concrete backends. Product semantics depend on scientific state rather than solvers or execution implementations. Backends implement declarative work and operator interfaces and do not own modes, coordinates, weighting, normalization, or products.

There is one production engine behind the application-owned typed installed-implementation availability boundary. casa-imaging-application checks compiled and task-only requirements against the implementation installed in the build before any work. Capabilities whose owners have not landed are returned typed unavailable rather than delegated to an alternate implementation. CI enforces the permitted crate graph and rejects forbidden edges (ADR-0016).

docs.title: Compile, plan, and run boundary
docs.text:
compile(request) produces an immutable Compiled Problem containing logical science, an Observation Snapshot (a manifest of the selection; bulk samples remain bounded streams), required capabilities, coordinate and reconstruction contracts, measurement-equation and weighting contracts, a Numerics Contract, and a Product Contract. It contains no backend-specific prepared operator or resource allocation.

Planning binds the compiled problem to a backend and a Resource Policy; each phase is admitted against the host before it runs (ADR-0016 decision 4).

run executes only what was compiled and admitted. It does not silently recompile, perform capability routing, choose an unlisted backend, or fall back to another implementation.

docs.title: Measurement equation and weighting
docs.text:
Let X be the declared model-coefficient space and D the selected unweighted visibility-sample space. The complete logical measurement operator is A: X -> D. A* is its adjoint under explicitly declared inner products. W is the positive-semidefinite data metric containing flags, input weights, tapering, and globally derived uniform or Briggs density weights.

The authoritative normal right-hand side is b = A* W d. For model x, the authoritative normal residual is g(x) = A* W (d - A x), and the logical normal operator is H = A* W A.

Any phase transformation, spectral sampling, polarization or Mueller mapping, channel integration, or direction-dependent response that affects both prediction and imaging belongs to a paired operator or explicitly paired composition. Data-only interpolation may not bypass the adjoint contract.

Published normalization, PB correction, sensitivity division, residual scaling, restoring-beam convolution, blanking, and unit conversion belong to the Product Contract and its normalization rules. They are not silently folded into a backend adjoint.

docs.title: Geometry and polarization
docs.text:
Compiled Geometry owns coordinate frames, image-domain charts, requested output coordinates, user-visible facet and outlier definitions, and deterministic transform specifications. It does not own sample-sized UVW, frequency, phase, or pointing arrays. Selected Observation streams evaluate per-sample coordinates from the compiled specifications.

Facet batching, tiling, halo sizing, and device partitioning are execution. W-, AW-, and facet convolution kernels are Measurement Operator implementations. Requested polarization coordinates belong to reconstruction; feed/correlation basis, parallactic-angle behavior, and Mueller response belong to the measurement equation and instrument response.

docs.title: Spectral semantics
docs.text:
Continuum and line share reconstruction, Measurement Operator, Normal State, product, and execution interfaces. Four distinct contracts define spectral behavior:

  • Spectral Coordinate Law defines native/output frames, rest frequency, velocity convention, epoch/direction/ephemeris dependencies, channel boundaries, and output WCS.
  • Spectral Sampling Operator defines paired channel integration or interpolation, coverage, flag/weight propagation, edge behavior, and the declared treatment of induced inter-channel covariance.
  • Reconstruction Basis defines constant, Taylor, channel-local, or other model coefficient functions.
  • Spectral Coupling Policy defines whether channels or basis blocks are independent, sequentially transformed, jointly reconstructed, regularized, or coupled through shared products such as a common restoring beam.

A cube uses a channel-local Reconstruction Basis but is not defined by that basis and is not an application loop around a continuum imager. Sequential continuum fitting/subtraction is an explicit visibility transform with fit channels, weights, model, provenance, and output-weight semantics (ADR-0011). Joint continuum-plus-line reconstruction is a different capability requiring a block normal operator with continuum-line cross terms and a separately accepted scientific decision.

docs.title: Side effects
docs.text: Read and write sets are explicit. Scientific products publish after the final complete-data reconciliation. Optional MODEL_DATA follows ADR-0008: the final pass predicts from the final model and writes the selected cells in place under casacore's table lock. Interruption may leave partial derived values, as in CASA; the next run recomputes them. Imaging adds no staging column, backup generation, content digest, or rollback mechanism beyond CASA-compatible table behavior.

docs.title: Major and Minor Cycles
docs.text:
A Major Cycle performs complete-data reconciliation over every selected sample using the logical operator and one frozen weighting generation. Complete-data excludes Minor Cycle approximations but does not imply bitwise identity, full materialization, one resident grid, or a shift-invariant PSF.

A Normal State Generation comprises the model generation, weighting generation, normal right-hand side, normal-operator or PSF approximation, sensitivity and sum-weight state, valid support, and Numerics Contract. It may be partitioned, streamed, tiled, sparse, or operator-backed.

A Minor Cycle consumes an immutable Minor Cycle View recording the approximation, valid domain, error or staleness bound, cycle threshold, and maximum admissible update. It returns a Model Delta and Solver Evidence and stops before violating that envelope. A final Major Cycle is mandatory before restoration and publication.

docs.title: Products
docs.text: A Product Contract and Product Graph own required/optional products, authoritative source generations, WCS and axes, units and normalization, per-plane/common-beam policy, residual scaling and restoration, PB/sensitivity correction, blanking and validity, cross-product dependencies, output schema, and the atomic replacement of each product. Backends may provide primitive transforms but may not define the meaning of image, residual, PSF, alpha, beam, mask, sensitivity, or PB-corrected products. Generation needs no content hashing or full-array reread to authorize publication (ADR-0014).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive: - code and verification follow the normal-equation and cycle mathematics - geometry, spectral sampling, reconstruction, normalization, and execution have distinct enforceable owners - continuum and line share infrastructure without claiming false semantic equivalence - each product is replaced atomically; MeasurementSet side effects follow CASA (ADR-0008)

Negative: - every solver and backend must satisfy explicit science and product contracts

Neutral / tradeoffs: - exact CLEAN component order and bitwise pixels are not preserved; agreement is judged by normalized tolerance

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
1. Preserve mode-oriented runners and share utilities.
  2. Translate LibRA/CASA C++ class and inheritance families directly.
  3. Build one broad imaging-run object owning science, resources, solvers, and products.
  4. Treat continuum, line, mosaic, and projections as independent top-level modes.
  5. Let a channel-local basis alone define spectral-line semantics.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text: This decision is enforced by: - tests: the T0 laws (weighted adjoint, linearity, spectral identity and nonidentity, cycle invariants) and T1 end-to-end tests of TESTING.md "Imaging tiers and evidence" - lint/import/dependency rules: scripts/check-imaging-dependencies.py rejects forbidden frontend, backend, observation, reconstruction, and product dependencies (ADR-0016) - CI checks: just arch-check - review trigger: stop before adding a second public run interface, an alternate stage path, backend-owned science/product semantics, or unpaired sampling - none / guidance only:

docs.title: Drift detection
docs.text: Suspect drift if: - a frontend or backend evaluates a science mode or writes a scientific product - Geometry owns sample-sized arrays or execution tiling - spectral interpolation is not represented in prediction and adjoint paths - a Minor Cycle mutates authoritative residual state or exceeds its view envelope - a capability can silently retry through another implementation - a solver or backend defines normalization, restoration, or output semantics

docs.title: ADR-0011: Continuum-line coupling
docs.text:
Status: retired Date: 2026-08-31 Truth class: normative Supersedes: Superseded by: ADR-0016 decision 11

ADR-0016 decision 11 removed the joint continuum-plus-line solver this ADR introduced; only the sequential continuum transform below still applies, and git history keeps the original text (#531).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: CASA's uvcontsub fits and subtracts the continuum in the visibility domain before line imaging (casatasks/src/private/task_uvcontsub.py, casatools/src/code/mstransform/TVI/UVContSubTVI.cc). casa-rs ports that transform. This ADR also accepted a joint continuum-plus-line reconstruction, which no longer exists in the code.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The sequential continuum transform is CASA's visibility-domain fit and subtraction, composed before independent channel-local line imaging. It fits each row and correlation over the fit channels with CASA's min/max frequency basis, subtracts the fit on the application channels, keeps the input flags and weights, and claims no propagated fit covariance. It is a visibility transform, not a joint reconstruction, and is never described as one. It lives in casa-imaging-operator (fit_and_subtract_continuum).

A joint continuum-plus-line solver would be a new capability with its own scientific contract and a new ADR (ADR-0016 decision 11).

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text: This decision is enforced by: - tests: continuum_transform_* and t46_sequential_uvcontsub_anchor_v1_matches_frozen_casa_row (a frozen CASA UVContSubTVI row) in crates/casa-imaging-operator/tests/continuum.rs - none / guidance only: retired; kept as the record of the sequential transform

docs.title: ADR-0014: Identity is ownership, without content attestation
docs.text:
Status: accepted Date: 2026-09-18 Truth class: normative Supersedes: Superseded by:
